Lessons.Title: New Room (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: New Room is an optional modeling lesson. Use area, missing lengths and reasonable design decisions to fit furniture into a room. Many arrangements can work. A floor plan is a map of a room viewed from above; it shows walls, doors, windows and furniture footprints. Explain your choices and assumptions instead of treating one layout as the required answer.

Warm-up — Notice and Wonder: inspect Tyler’s L-shaped floor plan in the companion. Identify the door, three windows and closet. Think quietly, discuss with a partner, and record notices and questions. The main room strip is 6 feet wide and 15 feet high; the lower-right extension is 4 feet wide and 5 feet high. The upper inside vertical length is 15 − 5 = 10 ft and the full bottom width is 6 + 4 = 10 ft. The closet has no printed side measurements; do not infer its exact footprint from the illustration.

Floor Plans: consider the furnished bedroom design, which includes a dresser, plants, piano, rug, bed, side table, desk and chair. Independently identify one thing you like and one thing you would change, with reasons. Discuss usable floor space and ways to move around the room. Plants close to the opening door might be bumped, and furniture placement affects chair access and walking routes. Practical and aesthetic reasons can both support a design; there is no unique required rearrangement.

Co-craft mathematical questions about the floor plan (MLR5). Compare questions with a partner, noting what they have in common and how they differ. Consider questions about comparing areas or how much room a rectangular item covers. Offer pre-cut first-party pieces or additional time if cutting is a barrier. A teacher checks the actual questions, reasoning and discussion rather than assigning a numeric score to personal design preferences.

New Bed and Desk: Tyler’s bed is 3 ft by 6 ft and his desk is 3 ft by 2 ft. Use the given L-shaped room measurements. Work in a group of two or four with grid paper, scissors and poster materials. The source allows either cutting out its supplied furniture shapes or creating your own diagram on grid paper. Here, draw the given room and footprints at one consistent labelled scale; use independently made cut-outs if useful. You may rotate furniture while preserving its dimensions.

Find the room area before deciding on a layout. A 6 ft by 15 ft main strip covers 90 ft² and a separate 4 ft by 5 ft extension covers 20 ft². The outer room area is 110 ft². An alternative split is a 6 ft by 10 ft upper part and a 10 ft by 5 ft lower part: 60 + 50 = 110 ft². These figures include the region where the closet is drawn; its separate footprint has not been dimensioned.

The bed covers 3 × 6 = 18 ft² and the desk covers 3 × 2 = 6 ft². If both are inside the room and do not overlap, their combined footprint is 24 ft². Subtracting only those two footprints from the outer area leaves 110 − 24 = 86 ft². Label this as the gross remainder after the bed and desk only. It is not a fully specified usable-space answer: the fixed closet has no supplied dimensions, and chair/door circulation choices need a stated interpretation. Do not silently invent a closet area or deduct an unspecified walkway as if it were furniture.

Try different arrangements. Keep the furniture within the room, avoid overlapping the bed and desk, consider the existing closet and door swing, and explain space to walk and use a chair. The two original questions ask where the furniture should go and what area is not covered by furniture. State exactly which footprints you counted and how you treated the closet. A teacher reviews the drawing, assumptions and reasoning; a typed 86 alone cannot establish that the plan fits or answers all practical considerations.

Create a labelled poster showing your layout, scale, recovered side lengths, room and furniture areas, and your interpretation of uncovered floor. Organize the work so another group can follow it. Gallery walk: half the class explains posters while the rest visits and asks questions. Use a five-minute round, move to another poster after about two minutes, then swap roles and repeat. Share a practical choice, a different valid arrangement and what made movement easier. Actual discussion and authorship remain teacher-reviewed.

Lesson synthesis: explain why many floor plans can work even when the room and furniture areas stay the same. Discuss door access, chair space and paths around the bed. Reflect on any unfinished area reasoning and explain how multiplication or a different rectangle split helped. Suggested centers are Five in a Row: Multiplication, stage 2 (factors 1–9), and supporting Five in a Row: Addition and Subtraction, stage 8 (add within 1,000 with composing).

For separate first-party practice, design an 8 ft by 10 ft rectangular bedroom using a 3 ft by 6 ft bed and a 3 ft by 2 ft desk. Specify door and window positions and make reasonable access choices. Label the plan and explain the floor not covered by those two items; the drawing and practical choices require teacher review.

New Edulytics exit task: a different 8 ft by 10 ft rectangular room contains only a 2 ft by 5 ft bed and a 2 ft by 3 ft desk. Draw a non-overlapping arrangement inside the room and explain door/chair access assumptions. The numerical floor area not covered by these two items is 80 − 10 − 6 = 64 ft². Your teacher still checks the plan. The original optional lesson has no listed publisher Cool-down; this is an independently authored Edulytics exit task.

KeyConcepts.Title: A floor plan is a model
KeyConcepts.Definition: A plan represents the room and furniture footprints from above.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use one labelled scale and preserve dimensions when rotating furniture.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 3 ft by 6 ft bed can rotate while keeping its 18 ft² footprint.

KeyConcepts.Title: Find composite room area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Non-overlapping rectangles can cover the room outline.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply each part and add areas once.

KeyConcepts.Title: State what uncovered means
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area left after selected footprints may differ from usable circulation space.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Name every footprint and do not invent missing closet measurements.
KeyConcepts.Example: 86 ft² is only the remainder after subtracting the given bed and desk from the outer room.

KeyConcepts.Title: More than one design can work
KeyConcepts.Definition: The same room and furniture areas permit different arrangements.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check fit, non-overlap, access and a reasonable explanation.
KeyConcepts.Example: A correct area alone cannot prove a door opens or a chair fits.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two room decompositions
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the area inside the outer L-shaped room boundary.

WorkedExamples.Title: Given furniture footprints
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the bed and desk areas.
Steps: For a non-overlapping arrangement their total is 24 ft².
WorkedExamples.Answer: 18 ft² for the bed and 6 ft² for the desk.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both items must actually fit inside the drawn room; area totals alone are insufficient.

WorkedExamples.Title: A conditional remainder
WorkedExamples.Question: What remains after subtracting only the new bed and desk?
WorkedExamples.Method: State the footprint assumption before subtraction.
Steps: Given bed and desk cover 18+6=24 ft² if disjoint.
Label this as remainder after those two items only, before any deduction for an undimensioned closet.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 86 ft² under the stated two-item-only assumption.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the closet interpretation, door/chair access and actual layout;86 is not a unique complete usable-space answer.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independent exit task
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the uncovered area of the separate rectangular room.
WorkedExamples.Method: Subtract only the explicitly listed non-overlapping items.
WorkedExamples.Check: Draw a feasible arrangement and explain access; the numeric check does not grade the design.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating one furniture arrangement as the only correct answer.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source problem has many possible designs.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check each plan’s fit, access and explanation against the same room and item dimensions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Saying enough total area guarantees furniture fits.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A footprint can cross a wall or block movement despite a sufficient total area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Inspect the actual scaled positions, rotations, door swing and chair access.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calculating an exact closet area from the picture.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State what is unknown and explain the footprint assumption; do not measure the display to invent a value.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using 86 ft² as an unconditional complete answer.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It subtracts only the bed and desk from the outer room and does not resolve the closet or practical access.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the two-item-only remainder and have the teacher assess the original plan and interpretation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtracting bed and desk areas while their drawn positions overlap.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The overlapping footprint would be deducted twice.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a non-overlapping arrangement or account for any overlap explicitly.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Submitting a number instead of a poster and discussion.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original task also requires a plan, organized reasoning and gallery explanations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show the labelled design, areas, assumptions and actual group work for teacher review.

SummaryPoints: A floor plan models room and furniture positions from above.
The outer source room area is 110 ft²; the bed covers 18 ft² and the desk 6 ft².
86 ft² is conditional on subtracting only those two footprints, not a fully specified usable-space result.
The closet lacks dimensions; state assumptions rather than inventing measurements.
Try several arrangements and check fit, non-overlap, door/chair access and walking routes.
Create a labelled poster, explain and compare designs; teacher reviews actual authorship and discussion.
